title: Judah and Tamar
summary: Judah leaves his brothers, marries a Canaanite woman, and has three sons. When his first two sons die after marrying Tamar, Judah withholds the third, so Tamar disguises herself, conceives by Judah himself, and exposes his failure with the pledge he left her. Judah confesses that she is more righteous than he is, and she gives birth to twins, Perez and Zerah.
story: The Joseph story has just begun: Joseph's brothers have sold him, and Jacob mourns a son he thinks is dead. Then the narrator turns away from Egypt and follows Judah, the brother who proposed selling Joseph for silver (37:26-27). The chapter can feel like an interruption, but it does two things the larger story needs. It shows Judah at his worst, careless of his family and quick to condemn a woman for what he himself has done, so that his later offer to become a slave in Benjamin's place (44:18-34) reads as a real change of heart. And it preserves the line that God's promise will travel along. Perez, born at the end of this chapter, is an ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18-22), and through David of the kings of Judah. The family that carries the promise to bless all nations is not a family of saints.
historical:
The chapter is set in the southern hill country and the Shephelah, the lower foothills between the Judean highlands and the coastal plain. Adullam, Chezib, and Timnah are towns in that region that later appear in Judah's tribal territory (Joshua 15). Judah "left his brothers" and settled among Canaanites, which fits the picture Genesis gives of the patriarchs as herders living alongside settled local peoples. The chapter covers many years (the births and growth of three sons, two marriages, and "a long time" in verse 12), so it overlaps with the years Joseph spends in Egypt rather than following them in strict order.

Genesis gives no fixed date for these events. Those who hold to an early date for the patriarchs place them in the first half of the second millennium BC; many other scholars think the stories took their written form much later. The same debate over the composition of Genesis noted elsewhere applies here.
cultural:
The key custom is levirate marriage (from the Latin levir, a husband's brother). When a man died without a son, his brother married the widow, and the first son was counted as the dead man's heir, carrying on his name and inheriting his share of the family land. Israel's law later regulated the practice in Deuteronomy 25:5-10, and the book of Ruth shows a wider form of it; law collections from the Hittites and from Assyria also contain provisions of this kind. For a childless widow it was her security and her place in the family. Onan's sin is that he takes the privileges of the arrangement while refusing its purpose, because a son for Er would reduce his own share of the inheritance. Judah's sending Tamar back to her father's house leaves her in limbo: bound to his family, but with no husband and no child.

The pledge Tamar asks for is telling. A seal (often a small cylinder or stamp carved with its owner's mark) was worn on a cord, and a staff could also carry distinctive markings; together they were something like a signature and an ID card. Sheep-shearing was a festive time of feasting (compare 1 Samuel 25). Hirah's word for the woman, qedeshah (verse 21), differs from the ordinary word for prostitute used in verse 15; scholars debate whether it refers to prostitution connected with a shrine, which older scholarship assumed was widespread, or simply to a woman of that status, since clear evidence for sacred prostitution in Canaan is disputed. The sentence of burning in verse 24 treats Tamar as a betrothed woman who has been unfaithful to Judah's family; Judah acts as head of the clan with power of life and death.
literary: The chapter is a tightly built short story whose hinge is recognition. In 37:32-33 Judah and his brothers sent Jacob a bloodied robe and asked him to examine it, and Jacob "recognized it"; here Tamar sends Judah his seal, cord, and staff with the words "Please examine them", and "Judah recognized the items." The deceiver of his father is now deceived with a young goat, the same animal whose blood stained Joseph's robe (37:31). Clothing marks each turn: Tamar removes her widow's garments, puts on a veil, and then puts the widow's garments back on. The story moves from Judah's power to Tamar's quiet planning, and its climax is Judah's own verdict, "She is more righteous than I." The closing birth scene, with a scarlet thread and a younger twin who breaks out first, echoes the struggle of Jacob and Esau (25:24-26) and Genesis's repeated reversal of the firstborn's place.

outline.t: Judah settles among Canaanites and has three sons
Er and Onan die, and Tamar is sent away to wait
Tamar's disguise at the road to Timnah
Judah condemns Tamar and then confesses
The birth of Perez and Zerah

doctrines.note: God is named only in the deaths of Er and Onan, yet the chapter ends with the birth of the ancestor of David. God keeps his promise through a family's failures and a widow's desperate plan, without approving of either.

Judah's sins are ordinary ones: neglect, self-protection, a double standard, and quick condemnation of someone else. The chapter shows how easily a person condemns in another what he has hidden in himself.

Judah's confession in verse 26 is the turning point of his life in Genesis. He owns the fault publicly, names the wrong he did to Tamar, and changes his behavior, which prepares for his self-giving speech in chapter 44.

words.note: Nakar, to recognize or examine closely. The same verb appears when the brothers ask Jacob to examine Joseph's robe (37:32-33) and later when Joseph recognizes his brothers while they do not recognize him (42:7-8). In this chapter it turns the story: the one who deceived by a garment is now confronted by his own belongings.

Yabam, to act as a brother-in-law, that is, to perform the levirate duty. The verb names a family obligation, not a personal preference: the living brother raises up offspring in the dead brother's name. It explains both Judah's command and the seriousness of Onan's refusal.

Tsadaq, to be righteous or in the right. Judah's words "She is more righteous than I" do not approve every step of Tamar's plan; they declare that in the dispute between them she was in the right, since she pursued the family's obligation that Judah had neglected. Righteousness here is covenant faithfulness to one's obligations.

Perez, from a verb meaning to break through, so the name means something like breach or breakthrough. The midwife's words give the pun. Perez heads the line that leads to Boaz and David (Ruth 4:18-22), and his clan was well enough known that Ruth 4:12 uses "the house of Perez" as a blessing.

christ: Matthew's genealogy of Jesus begins with Abraham and, among its long list of fathers, includes four women before Mary; Tamar is the first: "Judah was the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar" (Matthew 1:3). Matthew does not explain why he includes her. Many readers note that each of these women stands at an irregular or scandalous point in the line, and several were outsiders to Israel, which suggests that the Messiah's family history was not tidy and that God's mercy reached beyond it. The chapter also begins the story of Judah, from whom the kings of Israel will come (49:10), and whose tribe produces David and, in the New Testament's telling, Jesus, called "the Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5). The link is not a hidden prophecy in Genesis 38; it is a family line that God kept alive through people who did not deserve to carry it.

hard.q: Why does Scripture tell a story like this, and is Tamar being praised for deception?
hard.a:
The story is uncomfortable on purpose. Genesis does not polish its patriarchs, and here the man whose name will be given to a tribe and a kingdom uses a woman he takes to be a prostitute and then orders his daughter-in-law burned. Readers have taken Tamar in different ways. Many Jewish and Christian interpreters have honored her as a woman who, denied justice by the one responsible for her, risked her life to secure a child for her dead husband's line, and they note that Judah himself declares her more righteous. Others stress that the narrator reports rather than endorses her method, and that the Bible elsewhere forbids the union (Leviticus 18:15). Both readings agree on the main point: the judgment the text pronounces falls chiefly on Judah, and God's purposes go forward through a situation made by human wrong.

A second question concerns Onan. Some Christian traditions have read verses 9-10 as a teaching against contraception as such; others argue that the sin the text identifies is Onan's refusal of his duty to his brother's widow while he used her. The chapter itself stresses the refusal to produce offspring for his brother.

questions: Judah condemns Tamar before he knows the truth about himself. Where are you quickest to judge in others what you excuse in yourself?
Tamar was left without recourse by the person responsible for her. What does this chapter suggest about how God views those whom powerful people neglect?
Matthew included Tamar in Jesus' family tree. What does it mean to you that the Messiah's ancestry includes stories like this one?
